system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-10-29 15:51:00 to 2179-10-31 18:12:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease and multiple prior abdominal surgeries was admitted with abdominal pain and diarrhea consistent with a disease flare. Initial labs showed acute kidney injury, dehydration, and nongap metabolic acidosis, all secondary to fluid loss from diarrhea. CT imaging revealed fecal loading and mild stranding in the distal ileum, improved from prior studies, with no obstruction or hernia. He was treated with IV fluids, increased prednisone to 40 mg daily, and supportive care. His symptoms improved, labs normalized, and he tolerated a regular diet. Stool studies ruled out infection. He was discharged home on continued prednisone, a short course of pain medication, and instructions to follow up with gastroenterology.
problems: Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

# Abdominal Pain/Flank pain. 
The patient presented to the emergency department with diffuse 
abdominal and flank pain, accompanied by diarrhea. The patient 
stated that his pain was inconsistent with his previous ___ 
flares (the last of which he had been discharged for a week 
prior), but that it felt somewhat more like his prior kidney 
stones. His prior CT abdomen from his last admission did not

admitted to the general medicine floor for further workup, and 
his pain was only partly responsive to pain medication. He was 
seen by GI and started on IV steroids; however, his normal ESR

demonstrated no obstruction, and improvement of inflammation 
relative to his last admission, strongly suggesting against a 
renewed ___ flare. The patient was restarted on the 
prednisone taper with which he had last been discharged. 
Although the patient continued to have frequent loose stools, he 
stated that this was at his baseline. Prior to discharge, the 
patient tolerated clears and full liquids. However, he had 
considerable discomfort after attempting to start a regular 
diet, thus we recommended that he stay on a low residue diet for 
several days after discharge.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure to take care of you here at ___. You were 
admitted to the hospital for diarrhea and abdominal pain.  The 
most likely cause of your symptoms is gastroenteritis, an 
inflammation of your gastrointestinal tract, most likely due to 
a viral infection. Though these infections are uncomfortable, 
they are usually self-limited, and resolve without antibiotics.

During your stay you had an x-ray and a CT scan of your abdomen 
which did not demonstrate an obstruction and actually 
demonstrated improvement in your inflammation and there was no 
concern for Crohns flare. 

No changes have been made to your medication regimen.  You are 
still to take the prednisone you were given for your most recent 
___ flare, 40mg by mouth daily. You should continue this 
dosage 
until you see your gastroenterologist Dr. ___ will 
taper down your dose over time.

At this time, it was decided that you should return home to a 
soft, low-residue diet until your symptoms improve.  Should your 
pain increase, you should try waiting a brief period before 
eating again, and at that point begin with several meals of 
clear liquids (water, ginger ale, jello), before advancing to a 
diet of soft, low-residue foods. If you can only tolerate clear 
liquids for several meals in a row, contact your doctor.

If you begin to feel feverish, chills, or see blood in your 
stool or vomit, please contact your doctor or go directly to the 
nearest emergency room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain and diarrhea. It started a few hours after I ate at a cookout yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. How often are you having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Every 30 minutes or so. And I can see undigested food in the stool. No blood, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I feel a bit feverish, but no chills or shaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You were just discharged a week ago for a Crohn’s flare—does this pain feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s sharper. And it’s more in my lower back, kind of like my old kidney stone pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We did a renal ultrasound in the ER—no stones. But we’ll check a CT to be sure nothing’s changed with your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been on prednisone since last time—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the 40 mg daily until you see your GI doctor. We’re not stopping it unless we’re sure this isn’t a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t want to go through another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can. For now, we’re giving IV fluids and some pain medication to keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back—white count is normal, and markers of inflammation like CRP and ESR are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right? Not a Crohn’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Those markers are usually high during a flare. This suggests it’s less likely to be active Crohn’s inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what’s causing the pain and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still working on that. Your CT is scheduled for tomorrow. But given the timing after the cookout, we’re thinking it could be gastroenteritis—maybe a viral infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like food poisoning? But I only ate a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t take much. Viruses can be very contagious. And with your history, your gut might react more strongly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have results from your CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. There’s no abscess, no obstruction, and no new inflammation. In fact, the area of thickened bowel from your Crohn’s looks better than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The CT confirms it’s not a flare. The pain and diarrhea are likely from a gastrointestinal infection—gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably not. Most cases are viral and get better on their own. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and let your body heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a little broth earlier. Felt okay. Can I eat more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try clear liquids for now—water, broth, ginger ale. We’ll advance slowly. Last time you tried regular food, it caused discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that didn’t go well. How long should I stay on liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until your bowel movements slow down. Then we’ll move to soft, low-residue foods—like toast, rice, applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look better. Kidney function is normal, and you’re not dehydrated anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit better, but still crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing the pain. But the trend is positive. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the prednisone as before—40 mg daily—until you see your GI doctor. They’ll taper it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use loperamide as needed. But focus on hydration and a low-residue diet for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you with a short supply of pain meds, just in case. But call us if you develop fever, chills, or blood in your stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my GI appointment next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stay on track with that. They’ll help manage your Crohn’s and adjust your treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease and multiple abdominal surgeries was readmitted three days after discharge for a recent flare, presenting with acute abdominal pain, flank discomfort, and frequent diarrhea. He reported symptom onset after attending a cookout, with stools containing undigested food. Initial concern was for a recurrent Crohn’s flare, but labs showed normal inflammatory markers, and CT imaging revealed improvement in prior ileal wall thickening with no obstruction or abscess. Renal ultrasound ruled out nephrolithiasis. The clinical picture and imaging supported a diagnosis of gastroenteritis, likely viral. The patient was managed with IV fluids, pain control, and dietary advancement from clear liquids. He improved clinically, maintained stable vital signs, and was discharged home on continued prednisone, a low-residue diet, and instructions for follow-up with gastroenterology.
